bib.title: Chapter 12. Dynamic Scheduling, CUDA Graphs, and Device-Initiated Kernel Orchestration (AI Systems Performance Engineering)

question: How can kernel launch, scheduling and multi-GPU communication be orchestrated on the device so the GPU never idles waiting for the CPU?

results.claim: A warp-batched atomic work queue halves runtime of an imbalanced kernel versus static per-thread assignment.
results.setup: Microbenchmark, N = 1<<20, per-thread work = idx % 256 (sin/cos loop); GPU model, runs and repeats not stated.
results.quote: the statically assigned kernel took about 200 ms, whereas the dynamic-queue version ran in roughly 100 ms
results.note: Gain stated as 10%-20% for moderate imbalance in the body, but 'typically between 10% and 30%' in Key Takeaways.

results.claim: Illustrative: capturing a 3-kernel pipeline in a CUDA Graph cuts iteration latency by 25%.
results.setup: Table 12-1, 100 iterations of A->B->C; baseline uses 300 launches and 300 cudaDeviceSynchronize calls; chapter says values are illustrative.
results.quote: The numeric values in all metrics tables are illustrative to explain the concepts.
results.note: Key Takeaways generalise to 'often a 20%-30% latency reduction'.

results.claim: Device-initiated graph launches have roughly 2x lower launch latency than host-side graph launches, flat in graph size.
results.setup: No benchmark, hardware or source given.
results.quote: have shown roughly 2× lower launch latency compared to equivalent host-side graph launches

results.claim: Illustrative: device-launched child kernels (dynamic parallelism) cut runtime by about 25% and idle by about 35 points versus host launches.
results.setup: Table 12-2, parent plus 2 children; host launches 3 vs 1; per-launch overhead ~20 us vs ~25 us; GPU idle ~40% vs ~5%.

results.claim: Default pending device-launch limit for dynamic parallelism is 2,048, configurable.
results.quote: By default, CUDA allows 2,048 outstanding device launches at one time.

results.claim: A graph can have up to 120 fire-and-forget graphs and 255 pending tail launches; only one pending self-tail-launch.
results.quote: You can have up to 255 pending tail launches enqueued in a CUDA Graph.
results.note: The 120 limit: 'A graph can have up to 120 total fire-and-forget graphs during the course of its execution.'

results.claim: Batching atomics (8 or 16 per grab) removes most contention; atomic_transactions_per_request near 1.0 means no contention.
results.setup: L2-cache atomics on modern GPUs; no measurement given.
results.quote: modest batch size of 8 or 16 can eliminate most contention due to the high L2 bandwidth

limits: All metrics tables are illustrative, not measured; real benchmarks are in the book's GitHub repository.
Microbenchmark gives no GPU model, repeats or variance.
Chapter says PyTorch has no API for conditional graph nodes or device-side work distribution; custom C++ needed.
Device launch overhead is about the same as host launch, so DP may lose for small kernels.
practices: Batch atomicAdd per warp (one leader atomic, __shfl_sync broadcast) to cut L2 contention (Atomic Counters).
Use a persistent warp-level atomic work queue when profiling shows idle SMs from uneven per-task runtimes (Atomic Queues).
Capture fixed pipelines in CUDA Graphs; preallocate memory, warm up before capture, keep static addresses (CUDA Graphs).
Capture one graph per batch size and pad inputs, as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM do (PyTorch, Inference Engines, and CUDA Graphs).
Capture at maximum size and use cudaGraphExecUpdate for changed parameters instead of recapturing (Dynamic Graph Update).
Use tail launch when the parent needs the graph's results; fire-and-forget for side tasks (Device-Initiated CUDA Graph Launch).
Use conditional graph nodes (IF/IF-ELSE/WHILE/SWITCH) to keep branching on the GPU; set the condition from one thread (Conditional Graph Nodes).
Use dynamic parallelism only when new work emerges from data at runtime; otherwise prefer device-launched graphs (Dynamic Parallelism).
Always overlap communication with compute; use NVSHMEM fine-grained signals rather than nvshmem_barrier_all (Orchestrate Across Multiple GPUs).
Capture NCCL collectives in graphs only with identical sequence and communicator on all ranks (Capturing Multi-GPU Collectives).
Choose by roofline: memory-bound gets overlap and lower precision; compute-bound with overhead gets fusion, persistent kernels, graphs; in-between gets concurrency (Roofline-Guided Scheduling).

terms.definition: A global atomic counter with atomicAdd used to hand out work dynamically across warps.
The child graph begins executing immediately and concurrently with the launching parent kernel.
Defers execution of the graph until the launching kernel reaches a synchronization point or completes.
A variation of fire-and-forget in which the launched graph executes as a peer to the parent graph, in the parent's stream environment.
Embeds control flow (IF, IF/ELSE, WHILE, SWITCH) in a CUDA Graph, decided on the GPU from a condition handle.
Lets a running parent kernel decide on the fly how many child kernels to launch.
NVIDIA library treating each GPU as a processing element in a partitioned global address space, with one-sided device-initiated put/get.
